name: Rivals + feature matrix + URL check
new_modules: PackPlate 4-feature yes/no/unknown matrix; two-model/URL rule inline
text:
You are a market analyst. We are four graduate students with ONE MONTH to build AND test this product, at roughly ten hours per person per week. Nothing you propose should assume a longer timeline. PackPlate:

PackPlate is a website that helps NC State students decide where to eat on campus. It collects dining hours, menus, and nutrition information from every campus dining location into one place, and lets students filter the menus by their dietary restrictions and goals, such as allergies, vegetarian, halal, or a protein target. Students can enter constraints for several people at once, so a group with different diets can find a location where everyone has something to eat. Students can also report how busy each location is, so others know what to expect before walking over. The information comes from what NC State Dining publishes, and the site shows when that information is incomplete rather than filling in gaps. It is aimed at students on meal plans, especially those living on campus who eat most of their meals in the dining halls.

List the ten closest competing products. Table one: product | category
(official university dining app / nutrition tracker / campus life app /
restaurant-finder / crowd/wait-time app / other) | who uses it | main
strength | main weakness | price | evidence URL.

Table two, per product, yes/no/unknown: does it (a) combine menus + nutrition
+ hours for one campus, (b) filter by MULTIPLE people's diets at once,
(c) show crowd/busyness, (d) admit when its data is missing?

Rules: no invented products. If unsure it exists, leave it out. Every product
needs a real URL or mark it unconfirmed. If you cannot support a claim, write
"unknown" — never fill a cell with something plausible.

name: The gap, with receipts
runnable_note: the gap sentence is written by the team after reading P1's results, then runnable is set to true
text:
We claim this market gap: <<FILL IN: the gap in one sentence>>

Interrogate it, using the evidence below.

VERIFIED EVIDENCE (checked against the source):
- NC State Dining's allergy disclaimer states that because of the number of
  meals served and food product changes from their vendors, it cannot be
  guaranteed that every allergen in the food served will be identified and
  labeled. https://dining.ncsu.edu/location/case/
- As of 28 July 2025, NC State moved menus and nutrition out of the OnCampus
  app into a separate web portal, while hours stayed in the app and on the
  website, so students now check two places.
  https://dining.ncsu.edu/news/dining-menus-no-longer-in-oncampus-app/07-25-2025

COLLECTED COMPLAINTS. NC State sources first; anything from another
university is labelled as such.

NC STATE — OnCampus app reviews (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oncampus/id431844600)
- AdmiralVibe, 11 Sept 2023, 1 star, "Cmon guys". Wanted to see dining hall
  menus for their macros and could not. Calls the app a barely functioning
  dumpster fire and asks NC State to spend $100 of their tuition fixing it.
  Note the date: nearly two years BEFORE menus were removed from the app, so
  the feature was already failing while it still existed.
- Krackenkaren68, 16 Aug 2021, 1 star. Says the app crashes repeatedly before
  opening, and jabs that an engineering school should be able to make a
  working app.

NC STATE — the university's own release note, OnCampus v8.2.0, 26 July 2025
- NC State states that menus and nutrition details were disabled in the app's
  dining views because of changes in the NC State Dining software, and
  directs users to the website instead. HealthKit and food journal
  integration were disabled at the same time, to return once the data is
  available in the new software. So NC State had macro tracking tied to
  dining menus, and lost it.

NC STATE — Reddit r/NCSU, "Dining hall food"
(https://www.reddit.com/r/NCSU/comments/1kn8fqg/dining_hall_food/)
- A commenter answering how to check what is in the food explains that you
  open a dining hall's menu and click individual items to see the ingredient
  list. That is the official workflow, described by a student: per item,
  manually, one at a time.
- Spooky-man098 notes the halls differ sharply, saying Fountain has the most
  variety while Clark and Case have roughly four options total.
- Izzothedj, on eating vegetarian at NC State, says they ended up mostly
  eating salad, steamed vegetables and sides, and that better options exist
  elsewhere on campus but cost money.
- CAUTION: most of this thread is about FOOD QUALITY — bland, mass produced,
  one report of getting sick. PackPlate does not address any of that. Only
  the three items above are about finding information.

NC STATE — FoodFinder, NC State App Development Club, Fall 2025 – Spring 2026
(https://github.com/NCSU-App-Development-Club/FoodFinder)
- Six NC State students built an Android app specifically because of this
  problem. Their stated reason: NC State Dining switched menus to a new
  platform, which means hours and menus are now in different places, and the
  new site has UX problems. They set out to build something faster and more
  streamlined.
- NOTE: FoodFinder is also our closest competitor. It already does unified
  hours, menus and dietary restriction information. It is Android-only, and
  has no group filtering, no crowd levels, and no data-completeness
  reporting.

NC STATE — Technician, 22 Jan 2025, on religious dietary restrictions
(https://technicianonline.com/75807/news/campus-dining-provides-accommodations-for-students-with-religious-dietary-restrictions/)
- A doctoral student and Hindu YUVA president says the main vegan and
  vegetarian options on Centennial Campus come down to a black bean burger
  and pizza, and that many Hindu students avoid the burger over cross-contact
  fears. The piece also reports halal items are among the most frequently
  requested.

OTHER UNIVERSITIES — fragmentation. Not NC State; treat as supporting only.
- The Daily Texan, 27 Oct 2023. A UT Austin computer science student calls
  finding the dining menus inefficient and says the data is everywhere. Three
  roommates were annoyed enough to build their own app, UT Dining.
  https://thedailytexan.com/2023/10/27/ut-dining-app-makes-menus-more-accessible-to-students/
- Student op-ed, Medium, 2021. Argues there is no single place to check
  menus, nutrition, allergens or diet-specific options, that the information
  is scattered and hard to read, and that students who cannot tell what is
  being served order off campus instead of using the meal plan they paid for.
  https://medium.com/english-op-eds/crap-we-need-a-dining-app-8e5f5ceabd47
- UConn student health project. Interns did not know some dining halls closed
  at weekends or that dining accommodated allergies at all, and argue a
  better navigation system is needed.
  https://studenthealth.uconn.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/1709/2022/11/IWC-B-Dining-Paw-Passport.pdf

WHAT WE DID NOT FIND — state this plainly rather than leaving it out.
- No complaint, at NC State or anywhere else, about being unable to filter
  for SEVERAL PEOPLE'S diets at once. Our headline differentiator has no
  documented demand behind it.
- No complaint about not knowing how busy a dining hall is.
- The App Store sample is small and favourable: 43 ratings, 4.8 average.
- Counter-evidence exists. A 2014 App Store review from a freshman with
  allergies praises the app for showing what was safe to eat, and a student
  with a severe nut allergy quoted in Spokin's NC State campus guide says all
  dining hall items are labelled and she feels comfortable eating on campus.

1. CONFIRM: list five findable items that show the gap is real (reviews
   begging for it, dead products that tried, forum threads). Cluster the
   complaints into themes; quote one complaint verbatim per theme.
2. REFUTE: what would prove the gap is fake — an existing product we missed,
   or evidence nobody wants it? Search for this actively; do not just list
   confirming evidence.
3. Mark each item FOUND (with source) or NOT FOUND.

If the refuting evidence wins, say so plainly. A dead gap found now is cheaper
than one found at the poster session.

We are four graduate students with ONE MONTH to build AND test this product,
at roughly ten hours per person per week. A gap we cannot fill in that window
is as dead as one that does not exist — say so if that is the case.

name: Mission + metric + stakeholders
text:
A mission statement gives the WHY (challenge), WHAT (thing we build), SO WHAT
(benefit). Example of the form:

Online content can be emotionally overwhelming. Our app helps make sense of
it. Sentiment Analyzer Pro lets users analyze the emotional tone of text,
images, news, speech, and YouTube comments. Whether you track brand
sentiment, filter negativity, or just stay informed, the app makes emotional
insight fast and accessible. With a Chrome extension and improved UI, it is
now easier than ever to understand how content feels, not just what it says.

Facts about PackPlate:
- Users: NC State students on meal plans, especially those living on campus
  who eat most meals in the dining halls. Also groups of friends with
  different diets deciding where to eat together.
- Problem: dining hours, menus and nutrition are published in separate
  places, there is no way to search menus by dietary restriction, and no way
  to find a location that works for several people at once. Nothing shows how
  busy a location is.
- Features: hours, menus and nutrition for every campus location in one view;
  filtering by allergies, halal, vegetarian and protein target; the same
  filtering for several people at once; student-reported crowd levels;
  explicit flags where the published data is incomplete.
- Data source: only what NC State Dining publishes.
- Constraint: NC State does not guarantee its allergen labels are complete,
  so the product reports what is published rather than whether a dish is
  safe.
- Stack: Next.js with TypeScript for the frontend, a FastAPI (Python)
  backend, PostgreSQL for the database, a scheduled Python job for ingesting
  NC State Dining hours and menus, pytest for backend tests, and Docker for
  containerization if deployment needs it.

We are four graduate students with ONE MONTH to build AND test this.

Part 1: write three candidate missions, five sentences each. Banned words:
leverage, empower, seamless, revolutionize, cutting-edge, innovative, solution.
The SO WHAT of each must contain ONE measurable claim — a metric with a
baseline and a threshold, provable by four students in one week (e.g. "cuts
the time a group of three with different diets needs to agree on a dining hall
from X min to under Y"). Each must contain one concrete detail a rival could
not copy-paste.

Part 2: list the stakeholders. Go past customer/staff/admin — who pays, who is
harmed (name the allergic student), who owns the data (NC State Dining), who
maintains this at 3 a.m., who gets sued when it's wrong. Table: stakeholder |
what they fear | one design decision that wins them over.

name: Milestones + data-dependency
text:
The team: four grad students, ONE MONTH to build AND test, ~10 hrs/person/week.

Skills, stated honestly: All four of us are computer science master's
students. Between us we have experience with web scraping, databases,
TypeScript and Next.js, Python and FastAPI, and some design skills. What none
of us has built is a scheduled data pipeline that runs scraping scripts
automatically and keeps the data up to date on its own.

PackPlate depends entirely on one data source — what NC State Dining
publishes:
- Menus and nutrition: NC State Dining moved menus to CBORD NetNutrition, at
  https://netmenu2.cbord.com/NetNutrition/ncstate-dining. The page at
  https://dining.ncsu.edu/ads/menu-nutrition-portal/ is a shell that renders
  its content in the browser; the menu data itself comes from NetNutrition,
  NOT from dining.ncsu.edu. That matters for terms of use: dining.ncsu.edu's
  robots.txt disallows only /wp-admin/ and permits everything else, but it
  does not govern NetNutrition. MUST CHECK: netmenu2.cbord.com's robots.txt
  and CBORD's terms of use.
- There is already a working scraper. The NC State App Development Club built
  FoodFinder (https://github.com/NCSU-App-Development-Club/FoodFinder), an
  Android app with a Kotlin backend that scrapes NetNutrition for menus and
  dining.ncsu.edu for hours, once daily, into SQLite. Its scraper source is
  public. It also exposes a free, unauthenticated API at
  https://foodfinder-api.appdevncsu.org with routes for locations, menus,
  menu items with dietary flags, and hours. The authors invite reuse, asking
  only for a distinct User-Agent and respect for their Cache-Control headers.
  UNVERIFIED: whether that API returns full nutrition numbers (calories,
  protein, carbohydrates, fat) or only dietary flags, and whether it
  preserves the distinction between an item with no allergen and an item that
  was never analysed. Our data-completeness feature depends on that
  distinction.
- Hours: the dining locations page, https://dining.ncsu.edu/locations/, which
  does return hours and open/closed status in its HTML. Hours are also in the
  OnCampus app and in FoodFinder's /api/hours route.
- Known caveat: NC State's own allergy disclaimer states that because of the
  number of meals served and product changes from their vendors, it cannot be
  guaranteed that every allergen is identified and labeled. NC State's
  nutrition materials also include a "Not Analyzed" marker, so some items
  have no nutrition data at all.
- Known caveat: in July 2025 NC State's own app team disabled menus,
  nutrition, HealthKit and food journal features in the OnCampus app, stating
  the data was not available from the new dining software and that the
  features would return once it was. The university's own developers have had
  trouble getting this data.

Part 1 — data risk. Table: risk | likelihood | impact | how we'd detect it |
mitigation buildable in one month. Cover at least: source layout changes;
data stale/wrong; data incomplete (missing allergens); terms of use forbid
scraping; a field we rely on disappears; the third-party API we might depend
on goes away. Then name the single biggest point of failure and the smallest
thing we can build this month to survive it. Do not assume the data is clean,
complete, or legally free — cite the terms of use or write "must check".

Part 2 — milestones. Here is our draft, grouped BEFORE (what was done in
Project 1a) / NOW (this month) / FUTURE (Project 3):
- BEFORE: audited an existing full-stack food application we did not write;
  produced 20 evidence-backed use cases from its code; built a harness that
  runs the same prompts across several language models and compares them;
  found faults including an allergen check that was never enforced on the
  server.
- NOW: ingest NC State Dining hours and menus on a schedule; build dietary
  filtering with a three-state result (fits / conflicts / data incomplete);
  extend filtering to several people at once and return locations where
  everyone has an option; add student crowd reporting; test the filter
  against a hand-labelled set of menu items.
- FUTURE: use class schedules to suggest where to eat in a gap; coordinate
  pickup or delivery between students; predict busy periods from accumulated
  history; native mobile app.

Classify each REALISTIC / STRETCH / FANTASY against the hours above (not a
funded startup), and check each has a TEST, not just a build. For every
FANTASY, give the largest slice that would be REALISTIC.

name: Support material
new_modules: PackPlate-exposure focus (allergen labeling, scraping ToU, data-protection)
text:
We are building PackPlate for NC State students: it ingests dining hours,
menus, and nutrition, and filters them by allergies, halal/vegetarian status,
and protein targets. We are four graduate students with ONE MONTH to build
AND test it, at roughly ten hours per person per week.

What support material would change this design if we read it? Long list.
Center on our real exposure: food-allergen labeling and liability; the terms
of use / robots policy of the pages we scrape; data-protection rules for the
user constraints we store; accessibility (WCAG/ADA) for a public student site;
the licenses of our dependencies.

For each item: name a real, findable source; one sentence on which PackPlate
feature it touches; rate MUST-READ / SHOULD-READ / SKIM. We cite the must-reads
in the report.

Rank with the one-month budget in mind — a standard we could not possibly
comply with this month should be marked as such rather than listed as
MUST-READ.

name: Red team + allergen liability
runnable_note: auto-fills from P1, P3, P4 via <<FROM:>>; runs in the same pass
text:
You are hostile to PackPlate. Below: our mission, milestones, and market survey.

--- OUR MISSION STATEMENT CANDIDATES AND STAKEHOLDERS ---
<<FROM: P3>>

--- OUR MILESTONES AND DATA RISK ANALYSIS ---
<<FROM: P4>>

--- OUR MARKET SURVEY ---
<<FROM: P1>>

Note: the mission section above contains THREE candidate mission statements.
Attack the strongest one, and say at the start which you picked and why.

Attack on three fronts, strongest honest case, no strawmen:
1. Nobody wants it — the need is imagined.
2. They can't build it — one month too short, team too green. Argue against
   four graduate students at ten hours each per week, not a generic
   "software is hard".
3. Someone does it better — name who.

Then the sharp one: you are a plaintiff's lawyer and a parent of a student with
a severe nut allergy. PackPlate told the student an item was safe using NC State
Dining's published data, and the data was wrong. Build the strongest liability
case, then give the cheapest fix (UI change / data check / disclaimer)
buildable in one month, and name the one mitigation we MUST ship in v1.

For every attack, state the evidence that would defeat it — we'll go collect it
or concede.
